raw_response:
Well, it's that time again—October, just after I finished harvesting the summer maize and the last batch of chili. The wheat needs to go in soon, and I'm looking at the whole year ahead on my 10.1 mu. Seven mu I keep for wheat-maize double cropping—that's my foundation, feeds the family and brings in cash. The other 3.1 mu by the house is for chili, which my wife mostly manages. She's good at it, and when prices are decent it pays better than grain, but the picking is backbreaking work.

For the wheat, I'm planting around October 12th. I'm using Jinmai 22, same as the past five years. I buy fresh seed every two years and mix in some saved seed to keep costs down—this year I bought 12.5 kg per mu at about 35 yuan/mu. Some folks in the village switched to fancy new varieties, but I know this one. For fertilizer, I spread 50 kg of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu as base before planting, then at jointing in late March I topdress with 15 kg of urea. The extension fellow said 15 kg nitrogen per mu is the "scientific" rate, but I've been doing roughly this for twenty years and last year I got 420 kg/mu. Could I save 50 yuan by cutting back? Maybe. But if I cut back and the wheat turns yellow, I lose ten times that. Better to stick with what works. I irrigate three times: winter irrigation around December if the soil is dry, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. Pumping costs money—electricity isn't cheap—but skipping irrigation is asking for trouble.

The maize window is always brutal. After wheat harvest in early June, I've got maybe five days before I need the maize in the ground or I lose growing degree days. I hire Old Zhang's walking tractor for quick rotary tillage—50 yuan per mu—and I plant a hybrid, Yuecheng 168 or something like that, about 45 yuan per mu for the seed. I put 45 kg of compound fertilizer in the furrow at planting, then topdress 15 kg urea when the plants hit large trumpet stage. Maize is easier than wheat in some ways. I usually irrigate twice, maybe three times if it's a drought year like last year. I keep it to twice if I can—every irrigation run is another 60-70 yuan in diesel and electricity for the pump.

The chili is a different story. We transplant seedlings in late April. My wife starts them in a small nursery bed in March. We put down chicken manure plus about 30 kg of compound fertilizer per mu before transplanting, then another 10 kg at flowering. Chili needs more potassium than grain, so I try to get compound with a bit more K when I can, though the shop doesn't always have it. We spray more for chili too—herbicide at transplanting, then insecticide and fungicide two or three times because anthracnose will ruin you if you're not careful. My wife, my daughter-in-law, and even my granddaughter after school do the picking. It takes twenty-something days of family labor over the season for that 3.1 mu. We don't hire anyone for chili—family labor is "free," and hired hands would eat all the profit.

Cash is always tight. My son sends home about 2,000 yuan a month from his factory job in Shijiazhuang, which helps with the grandchildren's school fees and my mother's blood pressure medicine. But I don't like borrowing. I'm budgeting about 5,500 yuan for farm inputs this year—seed, fertilizer, diesel for the pump, pesticides, and Zhang's tractor. That leaves me a cushion. I'd rather sleep easy with a few hundred yuan in the drawer than squeeze out an extra 20 kg of yield.
